extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, law professors, policy analysts, and advanced law students interested in patent doctrine and patent policy
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and evaluation of doctrines and policy considerations governing improvement patents, claim drafting (e.g., Jepson claims), the reverse doctrine of equivalents, holdup/bargaining effects, and the welfare tradeoffs of patent breadth/length. Focuses on legal rules, case law, and economic implications for patent scope and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jepson claims / improvement patent identification
rubrics_metrics.description: A Jepson claim is a special claim format used to draft an improvement patent; 'strictly speaking only a patent drafted in Jepson format is an improvement patent.' A Jepson claim has the same effect as a judicial finding that a patented invention is 'dominated' by another invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of Jepson format signals that the claim is an improvement and affects claim construction and scope (see Pentec, Inc. v. Graphic Controls Corp.; R. Ellis, Patent Claims §197). The article also notes that the term 'improvement patent' is used more loosely to cover patents later found to be dominated by earlier patents. See 35 U.S.C. §101 for statutory provision relating to improvement patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse doctrine of equivalents — applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The reverse doctrine of equivalents can provide immunity from infringement even where there is literal infringement, but applies only when the accused device, though literally within claim language, is sufficiently different so that it does not perform in the same way as the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrine applies only where there is literal infringement; it is invoked when 'claims are written more broadly than the disclosure warrants.' Courts treat reverse equivalents as fact-intensive (sometimes a matter of fact, not law) and it has been 'rarely successfully asserted' by infringers. See Westinghouse v. Boyden Power Brake Co.; Texas Instruments v. USITC; SRI Int'l v. Matsushita (en banc) and commentary in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of improvements — obviousness (35 U.S.C. §103)
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvement is not patentable if it would have been obvious to one skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference to statutory obviousness standard: 35 U.S.C. §103 (1988). If an improvement would have been obvious, no patent should be granted on it — this is a threshold for exclusion from patent protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holdup problem — assessing bargaining/market power effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Holdup occurs when an owner of a complementary patent (the original patentee) can extract rents from an improver by leveraging the need to combine assets, potentially capturing substantial portions of the improver's surplus and causing inefficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the relative value contributed by the improvement vs the original patent (examples given where small vs very large improvements yield different welfare effects). Holdup can prevent introduction of improvements, cause delays, or raise consumer costs. The text recommends awareness of holdup when assessing remedies, scope, or policy (cites Calabresi & Melamed; Klein, Crawford & Alchian; empirical bargaining illustrations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory licensing as potential remedy (theoretical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compulsory licensing — allowing the improver to use the original invention in exchange for a 'fair' royalty — would likely be an efficient way to address holdup but is not part of U.S. patent law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article treats compulsory licensing as a theoretically efficient solution to holdup when an improvement must use a patented invention, but notes that U.S. law currently lacks such a mechanism; thus decision-makers must work within the 'second-best' choices of finding infringement or no infringement. See discussion and references to literature proposing compulsory licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use defense — scope and strategic impact
rubrics_metrics.description: An experimental-use defense may apply when a patented invention must be used to create an improved version, but its precise contours are unclear and are derived from case law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expanding the experimental-use exemption (advocated by some scholars) could significantly affect fields with substantial experimental work (e.g., biotechnology). The article cites Eisenberg and cases like Scripps Clinic v. Genentech as relevant authority and discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages and reasonable royalty apportionment for blocking patents
rubrics_metrics.description: In situations of blocking patents or complementary patent rights, the reasonable royalty must reflect an appropriate apportionment of the expected economic benefits between parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rights block each other, damages calculations (reasonable royalties) should apportion value of the combined invention appropriately; a subservient patentee may be liable for damages measured by the value of royalties under a license agreement. See Chisum §20.03[3] and cited cases (Water Technologies Corp. v. Calco; Oil Well Improvements Co. v. Acme Foundry & Mach. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal claim scope vs. functional/operational principle (infringement analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if an accused device falls within the literal language of a claim, there may be no infringement if the device operates on a substantially different principle or way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held no infringement where defendant's machines 'do not operate on the same principle as plaintiff's' even though the devices fall within literal claim language (cases: Leesona Corp. v. United States; Precision Metal Fabricators v. Jetstream Sys.; Mechanical Plastics Corp. v. Unifast Indus.). This supports narrowing claim scope by reference to function/principle in some contexts (related to the 'reverse equivalents' and claim-saving-by-specification doctrines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim breadth tradeoffs — breadth vs. deadweight loss and length
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing the breadth of a patent typically increases deadweight loss (especially as the patentee's market power grows); there is a tradeoff between breadth and length when designing patent rewards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic models suggest social-cost effective policy may adjust both breadth and length to attain desired rewards (citations to Gilbert & Shapiro; Klemperer). Broad claims have greater preclusive effects than longer duration; in some models infinitely-lived patents with adjusted scope could be considered, but there are cautions that excessive breadth can retard subsequent innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider social vs private returns when setting patent policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy choices about patent scope and related rules should account for the difference between social returns to innovation and private returns to patentees; social returns are often much larger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical literature cited indicates social rates of return on innovations often far exceed private returns (examples and studies cited). Because patents create social costs (deadweight loss) not borne by patentees, net-social-benefit analysis should inform patent scope and rules (citations include Mansfield, Bresnahan, Bernstein).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transaction costs and bargaining feasibility in licensing/improvement exchanges
rubrics_metrics.description: High transaction costs (identifying prospective improvers, valuing inventions, negotiating splits) can prevent efficient bargaining between pioneer patentees and improvers, undermining private solutions to holdup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies show licensing transaction costs can be substantial (examples: Contractor, Teece, von Hippel). Policy/regulatory choices should consider these costs; contractual remedies or assumptions that bargaining will solve hold-up problems are often unrealistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer narrower scope in close marginal scope cases to encourage improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: In close cases where scope doctrines are at issue, decision makers should opt for narrower patent scope to advance society's interest in encouraging improvements, while recognizing this may reduce pioneer incentives at the margin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article argues that the positive-sum aspects of allowing more competition for improvements favor narrowing the scope at the margins; this recommendation is tempered by recognition that narrower scope can reduce pioneer returns and thereby affect incentives to invent (numerical examples illustrate tradeoffs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be commensurate with specification / not broader than disclosure warrants
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims written broader than the disclosure warrants invite invocation of doctrines like reverse equivalents and may be vulnerable; claims should be commensurate with the written disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Newman observed reverse equivalents 'is invoked when claims are written more broadly than the disclosure warrants.' Drafting should avoid overbroad claims relative to the specification to reduce risk of equitable defenses or invalidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority and statutory bars (35 U.S.C. §102 family)
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority-of-invention rules and statutory bars limit entitlement to patents; e.g., priority depends on reduction to practice and earlier conception, and public use/publication/sale more than one year before filing can bar patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to 35 U.S.C. §102(g) (priority rules), §102(b) (one-year public use/sale bar) and supporting case law are included; practitioners should account for these temporal/privity rules when assessing patentability and prior art issues.
